lessons.title: Storage Requirements: Temperature and Humidity
lessons.body: Proper storage is critical to reduce post-harvest losses, which can reach 30-50% in Africa if onions are not stored well. Onions store best at 0-4Â°C with 65-70% relative humidity. However, in most African farms, cold storage is expensive and unreliable. Instead, you can use improved natural ventilation storage. Cure onions first: after harvest, leave them in the field for 2-3 days to dry, then move to a shaded, well-ventilated area for 2-3 weeks until necks are dry and skins rustle. For small-scale storage, use raised wooden pallets or shelves in a dark, dry room. Ensure good airflow: space onions in thin layers (no more than 15 cm deep) or hang in mesh bags. Avoid direct sunlight and rain. In humid areas, use a fan or dehumidifier if possible. Check regularly for soft or sprouting bulbs and remove them immediately. For larger scale, consider a solar-powered cold room; many African cooperatives share such facilities. Ideal storage life: 3-6 months for well-cured onions. Without proper storage, onions may sprout, rot, or lose weight. Keep rodents and insects out by sealing gaps and using traps, not poison near food. Remember: temperature and humidity control are your main tools to maintain quality and price.

lessons.title: Common Storage Diseases and Pests
lessons.body: Even with good storage, onions can be attacked by diseases and pests. The most common fungal diseases are neck rot (Botrytis), black mold (Aspergillus niger), and blue mold (Penicillium). Neck rot appears as soft, watery spots near the neck, often with gray mold. Black mold causes black powdery patches on outer scales. These spread in warm, humid conditions. To prevent, ensure onions are well-cured and stored dry. Remove infected bulbs immediately. Bacterial diseases like soft rot (Erwinia) cause foul-smelling, mushy bulbs; avoid wounding onions during harvest. Pests include onion thrips (tiny insects that cause silvery streaks), mites (which cause surface damage), and rodents. Thrips can be controlled by good ventilation and by hanging yellow sticky traps. For mites, keep humidity low. Rodents: use traps and keep storage area clean. In Africa, a common problem is the onion fly (Delia antiqua) in storage? Actually, onion fly is field pest, but in storage, beetles like the cigarette beetle can infest. Use diatomaceous earth (food grade) sprinkled around storage area to deter insects. Never use chemicals directly on onions intended for consumption. For organic control, neem leaves or garlic sprays can repel some pests. Regularly inspect stored onions every two weeks. Sort out soft, sprouting, or moldy bulbs. If you find many infected bulbs, sell them quickly for processing (e.g., puree) rather than losing all. Proper curing and dry storage are your best defenses.

lessons.title: Controlled Atmosphere Storage
lessons.body: Controlled atmosphere (CA) storage involves adjusting oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen levels to extend onion shelf life. Typically, onions are stored at 0-4Â°C with 1-3% oxygen and 5-10% carbon dioxide. This slows respiration, sprouting, and decay. However, CA storage is expensive and requires airtight rooms and gas control equipment. For most African smallholders, this is not feasible. But you can mimic some benefits with modified atmosphere packaging (MAP). Use perforated plastic bags or liners that allow some gas exchange but reduce oxygen. For example, store cured onions in 5-10 kg perforated polyethylene bags; this can extend storage by 2-4 weeks. Another low-cost method is vacuum storage: seal onions in airtight containers with a small oxygen absorber packet. This is practical for small quantities for home use or high-value markets. In Kenya and Nigeria, some commercial farms use solar-powered cold rooms with CA for export. If you are a cooperative, consider investing in a shared CA facility. But for most, focus on proper curing, ventilation, and cool, dry storage. CA is not a replacement for good curing. Always cure onions first. Also, different onion varieties respond differently; red onions often store longer than white. Test small batches before scaling up. Remember, CA requires monitoring: check gas levels daily and remove any spoiled bulbs. If you cannot afford CA, don't worry; good traditional storage can still give you 3-5 months.

lessons.title: Market Channels: Wholesale, Retail, and Direct
lessons.body: Selling onions profitably means choosing the right market channel. Wholesale: You sell large quantities to traders or wholesalers at farm gate or local markets. Price is lower but you sell fast. In many African countries, wholesale prices fluctuate; for example, in Nigeria, a 100 kg bag may sell for 20,000-40,000 Naira depending on season. Retail: You sell directly to consumers in small quantities at markets or roadside stalls. You get higher prices but need time and transport. A 1 kg bunch may sell for 500-1000 Naira in cities. Direct: Selling to restaurants, hotels, schools, or through community-supported agriculture (CSA) or online platforms. You can negotiate contracts and get better prices. For example, a restaurant may buy 50 kg weekly at a premium. To access these, form relationships and ensure consistent quality. Cooperatives can aggregate produce to meet large orders. Also consider selling to processors for value-added products (see lesson 6). Key tips: grade onions by size and quality; uniform onions fetch higher prices. Use clean, labeled bags. For retail, display attractively. For wholesale, ensure timely delivery. In Africa, mobile money (M-Pesa, Airtel Money) simplifies payments. Always have a backup channel: if wholesale prices crash, retail or direct can save you. Keep records of sales to identify best channels. Join farmer groups to share transport and market information. Remember, consistent supply and quality build trust and repeat business.

lessons.title: Pricing Strategies and Market Analysis
lessons.body: Pricing onions right is key to profit. First, know your costs: seeds, fertilizer, labor, storage, transport, and packaging. Add a 20-30% profit margin. But market forces matter. Do market analysis: visit local markets, check prices on radio, or use apps like Esoko or M-Farm. In East Africa, onion prices peak in dry seasons when supply is low. For example, in Tanzania, prices may double from harvest to off-season. Strategies: 1) Cost-plus pricing: calculate total cost per kg and add margin. 2) Competitive pricing: match or slightly undercut nearby sellers. 3) Value-based pricing: if your onions are organic or premium, charge more. 4) Dynamic pricing: adjust prices based on demand (higher on weekends). 5) Bulk discounts: encourage large buyers. Also consider storage: if you can store until prices rise, you gain more. But storage costs and risks exist. Use a simple break-even analysis: if storage costs 1000 Naira per bag per month and price rises by 5000 Naira after two months, it's worth it. Keep records of prices over time to predict trends. Join cooperatives to negotiate better prices collectively. Avoid panic selling at harvest when prices are lowest. Instead, sell part and store part. For direct markets, you can set higher prices due to freshness and traceability. Always communicate value: tell customers your onions are well-cured and chemical-free. Use social media (WhatsApp, Facebook) to advertise. Bartering is common; know your bottom line. Finally, be flexible; prices change, so review weekly.

lessons.title: Value-Added Products: Powders, Pickles, and Sets
lessons.body: Turning onions into value-added products increases income and reduces waste. Onion powder: Dehydrate sliced onions in a solar dryer or oven at 50-60Â°C for 6-8 hours until brittle. Grind into powder using a blender or mill. Store in airtight jars. 1 kg fresh onions yields about 100-150 g powder. Sell in 50g or 100g packets to supermarkets or online. Onion pickles: Slice onions, mix with vinegar, salt, sugar, and spices (e.g., turmeric, chili). Pack in sterilized jars. Pickles last 6-12 months. A 500g jar can sell for 3-5 times the price of fresh onions. Onion sets: Grow small bulbs (sets) for planting. Harvest when bulbs are 1-2 cm diameter, cure, and store. Sell to other farmers as planting material. Sets fetch high prices because they save farmers time. In Africa, demand for sets is growing. Also consider onion paste or puree: blend onions, cook, and package in sachets; sell to restaurants. For all products, ensure hygiene: wash hands, sterilize equipment, use clean water. Label with production and expiry dates. Get necessary permits from local authorities. Packaging matters: use attractive, sealed bags or jars. Market via local shops, social media, and farmer markets. Start small, test demand, then scale. Value-added products can double or triple your income from the same harvest. They also use smaller or damaged onions that would otherwise be discarded. Train yourself via online videos or local workshops. With simple tools, you can process onions at home. Remember, consistency in quality builds reputation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for storing onions?
quiz.explanation: Onions store best at 0-4Â°C to slow sprouting and decay.

quiz.q: What relative humidity is recommended for onion storage?
quiz.explanation: 65-70% relative humidity prevents rot while avoiding excessive drying.

quiz.q: How long should onions be cured before storage?
quiz.explanation: Curing for 2-3 weeks dries the neck and skin, improving storage life.

quiz.q: Which disease causes soft, watery spots near the neck of onions?
quiz.explanation: Neck rot (Botrytis) is characterized by soft, watery spots near the neck.

quiz.q: What is a common pest of stored onions?
quiz.explanation: Onion thrips can infest stored onions, causing silvery streaks.

quiz.q: How can you control mites in onion storage?
quiz.explanation: Mites thrive in humid conditions; keeping humidity low helps control them.

quiz.q: What is a safe organic method to deter insects in onion storage?
quiz.explanation: Food-grade diatomaceous earth is a safe, non-toxic insect deterrent.

quiz.q: How often should stored onions be inspected?
quiz.explanation: Regular inspection every two weeks helps remove spoiled bulbs early.

quiz.q: What does controlled atmosphere storage involve?
options: A) Adjusting oxygen and carbon dioxide levels
quiz.explanation: CA storage adjusts gas levels to slow respiration and extend shelf life.

quiz.q: What is a low-cost alternative to CA storage for smallholders?
quiz.explanation: Both modified atmosphere packaging and vacuum sealing can mimic CA benefits at low cost.

quiz.q: What percentage of oxygen is typical in CA storage for onions?
quiz.explanation: Low oxygen (1-3%) helps reduce respiration and sprouting.

quiz.q: Which onion variety often stores longer?
quiz.explanation: Red onions generally have better storage life than white onions.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of selling wholesale?
options: B) Fast sale of large quantities
quiz.explanation: Wholesale allows you to sell large volumes quickly, though at lower prices.

quiz.q: Which market channel typically gives the highest price per kg?
quiz.explanation: Direct sales to restaurants or hotels often fetch premium prices.

quiz.q: Why is grading onions important for marketing?
options: B) Uniform onions fetch higher prices
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Graded, uniform onions are more attractive and can be priced higher.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a farmer cooperative for marketing?
options: A) Shared transport and better prices
D) No need to grow onions
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives help aggregate produce, share transport, and negotiate better prices.

quiz.q: What should you know before setting onion prices?
quiz.explanation: Knowing both costs and market prices ensures profitable pricing.

quiz.q: What is a dynamic pricing strategy?
options: B) Adjusting prices based on demand
quiz.explanation: Dynamic pricing changes with demand, like higher prices on weekends.

quiz.q: Why might storing onions be profitable?
quiz.explanation: Off-season prices are typically higher, so storing can yield more income.

quiz.q: What is break-even analysis used for?
options: A) To decide if storage costs are worth it
quiz.explanation: Break-even analysis compares storage costs to potential price increases.

quiz.q: What is a value-added onion product?
quiz.explanation: Onion powder is a processed product that adds value to fresh onions.

quiz.q: How are onions dehydrated for powder?
options: B) Solar drying at 50-60Â°C for 6-8 hours
quiz.explanation: Solar drying at 50-60Â°C for 6-8 hours produces brittle onions for grinding.

quiz.q: What is the approximate yield of onion powder from 1 kg fresh onions?
quiz.explanation: Dehydration reduces weight; 1 kg fresh onions yields about 100-150 g powder.

quiz.q: What is a key ingredient in onion pickles?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar is essential for pickling, providing acidity and preservation.

quiz.q: What are onion sets?
quiz.explanation: Onion sets are small bulbs grown specifically for planting.

quiz.q: Why are onion sets in demand?
options: C) They are easier to store
quiz.explanation: Sets reduce the time from planting to harvest, appealing to farmers.

quiz.q: What hygiene practice is crucial for value-added products?
quiz.explanation: Sterilizing equipment prevents contamination and spoilage.

quiz.q: What should be included on value-added product labels?
quiz.explanation: Labels must show production and expiry dates for safety and traceability.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of value-added products?
quiz.explanation: Value-added products can use substandard onions and boost income.

quiz.q: What is a good way to market value-added onion products?
quiz.explanation: Multiple channels like social media, shops, and markets increase sales.
